stances.claim: The Judicial Affidavit Rule -- shortcutting direct examination -- is a proven reform: the Quezon City pilot reduced by two-thirds the time for witness testimony.
591 funded but vacant trial courts represent 26% of the organized trial court system -- filling them would increase judicial capacity by more than 25%.
The private meeting the author hosted -- producing an executive-legislative agreement on stable judicial compensation -- is a practical example of the creative dialogue needed between the branches.
The three reforms are interrelated: the first shortens trials, the second adds capacity, and the third raises quality by enticing better lawyers and insulating judges from bribery.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban surveys three interrelated judicial reforms. First, the Judicial Affidavit Rule (promulgated September 4, 2012; effective January 1, 2013), drafted by committees led by JJ Carpio and Abad: witnesses no longer give direct testimony through Q&A but instead submit affidavits in their language with translation, while the adverse party retains cross-examination rights; applies to all civil cases and criminal cases with a maximum 6-year penalty or with the accused's consent; a Quezon City pilot showed it reduced direct testimony time by two-thirds. Second, the vacancy problem: Drilon discovered at a Senate finance hearing that 591 trial courts (26% of organized courts) were funded but vacant, with their budget realigned as SAJ and other supplements for sitting judges. CJ Sereno (as JBC chair) committed to hasten short lists so all vacancies could be filled by 2015. Third, compensation stabilization: at a private meeting hosted by the author, Budget Secretary Abad and legislative leaders Drilon and Rep. Abaya agreed to fund stable monthly compensation for trial judges -- RTC judges at P128,198.66, MeTC judges at P119,209.66, MTC judges at P102,612-P110,925 -- eliminating the need for 'savings realignment.' The three reforms are interlocking: the first shortens trial time, the second adds 25%+ judicial capacity, and the third raises quality by attracting better lawyers and helping judges resist bribery. The column closes with a plug for the FLP Professorial Chairs launch on September 18.
